title: 2 Chronicles 23:12–21
context: Athaliah comes to the temple, cries treason, and is led out and killed away from the LORD’s house. Jehoiada renews the covenant that the people will be the LORD’s, the house of Baal is torn down, and temple worship is restored according to the law of Moses and David’s arrangements. The king is enthroned, and the city is quiet. The parallel is 2 Kings 11:13–20; Chronicles adds details about the singers, the Levitical order, and the gatekeepers. The notes report the violence with restraint. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about restoration and renewed loyalty to the LORD.

verses.text: When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she came to the people into the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Athaliah hears the people running and praising the king and comes to them in the LORD’s house. The usurper confronts the scene.

Arminian readers see her drawn by the noise of a restoration she did not foresee.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 11:13 speaks of the noise of the guard and the people; Chronicles mentions the people running and praising the king.

Reformed readers see God’s plan coming into the open. Both traditions read this as shared ground and name the difference in wording without resolving it.

verses.text: Then she looked, and behold, the king stood by his pillar at the entrance, with the captains and the trumpeters by the king. All the people of the land rejoiced and blew trumpets. The singers also played musical instruments, and led the singing of praise. Then Athaliah tore her clothes, and said, “Treason! treason!”
verses.arminianNotes:
She sees the king by his pillar at the entrance with captains and trumpeters, the people rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and singers leading praise; she tears her clothes and cries, “Treason! treason!” Her power collapses.

Arminian readers see joy replacing fear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles adds the singers, a detail not found in 2 Kings 11:14, in keeping with its interest in temple music.

Reformed readers see worship celebrating God’s faithfulness. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Jehoiada the priest brought out the captains of hundreds who were set over the army, and said to them, “Bring her out between the ranks; and whoever follows her, let him be slain with the sword.” For the priest said, “Don’t kill her in the LORD’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada commands the captains to bring her out between the ranks and kill anyone who follows her, but not to kill her in the LORD’s house. Reverence restrains even judgment.

Arminian readers see concern for the sanctity of God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse closely follows 2 Kings 11:15. The narrative reports the order without elaboration.

Reformed readers see the holiness of God’s house respected. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground and do not hold up the violence as a pattern for others.

verses.text: So they made way for her. She went to the entrance of the horse gate to the king’s house; and they killed her there.
verses.arminianNotes:
They make way for her, and she is killed at the entrance of the horse gate to the king’s house. Her reign ends.

Arminian readers see judgment coming on one who shed royal blood, as the text records it without elaboration.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 11:16 speaks of the horses’ entry; Chronicles calls it the horse gate. The exact location is not certain.

Reformed readers see God’s justice in the fall of a usurper. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground and report it with restraint.

verses.text: Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king, that they should be the LORD’s people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada makes a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king that they will be the LORD’s people. Covenant identity is renewed.

Arminian readers see a conscious, communal commitment to belong to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 11:17 describes the covenant as between the LORD, the king, and the people, and also between king and people. The wording differs.

Reformed readers see the people restored to their calling under God. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: All the people went to the house of Baal, broke it down, broke his altars and his images in pieces, and killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the people go to the house of Baal, break it down, smash its altars and images, and kill Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. False worship is removed.

Arminian readers see renewed commitment expressed in action.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse follows 2 Kings 11:18 closely. The text reports Mattan’s death without elaboration.

Reformed readers see restoration including purified worship. Both traditions read this soberly as narrative of reform, consistent with the 2 Kings 11 notes, without holding up the violence as a pattern.

verses.text: Jehoiada appointed the officers of the LORD’s house under the hand of the Levitical priests, whom David had distributed in the LORD’s house, to offer the burnt offerings of the LORD, as it is written in the law of Moses, with rejoicing and with singing, as David had ordered.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada places the temple officers under the Levitical priests whom David had organized, to offer burnt offerings as written in the law of Moses, with rejoicing and singing as David ordered. Worship is restored.

Arminian readers see order and joy returning together.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 11:18 says only that the priest appointed officers; Chronicles expands this with David’s arrangements and the law of Moses.

Reformed readers see worship ordered by God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He set the gatekeepers at the gates of the LORD’s house, that no one who was unclean in anything should enter in.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada sets gatekeepers at the gates of the LORD’s house so that no one unclean may enter. Holiness is protected.

Arminian readers see care for the purity of worship after years of disorder, as the people return to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
This detail appears only in Chronicles, which gives sustained attention to the temple’s gatekeepers.

Reformed readers see the purity of God’s house guarded according to his law. Both traditions read this as shared ground about reverent worship and do not press the verse further.

verses.text: He took the captains of hundreds, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land, and brought the king down from the LORD’s house. They came through the upper gate to the king’s house, and set the king on the throne of the kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada brings the captains, nobles, governors, and all the people, escorts the king from the LORD’s house through the upper gate to the palace, and sets him on the throne. The restoration is complete.

Arminian readers see broad consent.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 11:19 names the Carites, the guard, and the gate of the guard; Chronicles names nobles, governors, and the upper gate. The differences are noted, not resolved.

Reformed readers see David’s heir enthroned. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. They had slain Athaliah with the sword.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the people of the land rejoice, and the city is quiet, for Athaliah has been killed with the sword. Peace follows the end of tyranny.

Arminian readers see joy and rest returning to God’s people after a dark time.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse closely follows 2 Kings 11:20. The quiet city contrasts with the violence of Athaliah’s reign.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to David vindicated. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the LORD keeping his promise through the restoration of Joash.
